newsitem.title: USA: Hearing for U.S. Army officer said closed to public.
newsitem.headline: Hearing for U.S. Army officer said closed to public.

text.p: The U.S. Army has decided to close to the public a preliminary hearing to determine whether there is enough evidence to court-martial its top enlisted man on sexual misconduct charges, the Washington Post reported in Friday editions.
The newspaper quoted Army sources as saying the Army leadership and many officers would like to find way to resolve the charges against Sergeant Major Gene McKinney without a public trial.

But attorneys for McKinney, who faces 18 criminal charges including adultery and indecent assault, and Brenda Hoster, a former military aide whose allegations sparked the criminal probe, charged that the Army was trying to avoid bad publicity at their expense.
"It is clear the Army wants to avoid bad publicity," McKinney's defence attorney, Charles Gittins, told the paper.
McKinney recently requested that he be permitted to retire after intermediaries suggested the Army would welcome such an option. The Army has not responded to McKinney's request.

"It's very, very important that the public know what the evidence is in these cases and judge the merits for themselves," said Susan Barnes, an attorney representing Hoster. "Brenda Hoster has the guts to go public. The Army should, too."

The preliminary hearing is due to begin Monday. After the hearing, the convening authority will weigh the evidence and decide whether to proceed with a trial, change the charges against McKinney, or dismiss the case.

McKinney, who is 46 and married, is charged with committing adultery with one female soldier and propositioning three others. He is also charged with assault, indecent assault, making a threat, mistreatment of a subordinate and obstruction of justice.

The case against McKinney is the latest in a series of revelations about adultery and sexual harassment in the military. The Defence Department's preferred candidate to take over as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff had to withdraw his name from consideration after a firestorm erupted over his adulterous affair 13 years ago.
